image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A set of **strip plots / dot plots** (one-dimensional scatter plots), shown as **four vertically stacked panels**.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting by topic**: four separate horizontal panels, each for a different metric.
- **No stacking**.
- Within each panel, countries are shown as dots positioned along a single horizontal quantitative axis.
- A highlighted dot color is used to emphasize the **U.S.** relative to other countries.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Cellphone service cost in 2019 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis in the first panel |
| Annual hours worked in 2018 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis in the second panel |
| Health expenditures in 2017, share of G.D.P. | Quantitative | Position on x-axis in the third panel |
| Annual minimum wage in 2018 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis in the fourth panel |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual dots; text labels for selected countries |
| Panel topic / metric | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into four separate panels with titles |
| U.S. highlight status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (purple for U.S., gray for others) |

comments.raw_comment:
From the four dot plots given, you can see that the US has the highest cell phone service rates, as well as the highest health expenditures out of all the countries shown. On the other hand, the US is just about in the middle of the pack for the other two categories, which were annual hours worked and annual minimum wage. From these dot plots, I believe that the United States isn’t in the best place it could be since our cell rates are higher and our annual wages are severely lacking compared to countries like Ireland and Australia. Something else I noticed was that the dot plots didn’t always include the same countries. I wonder why the creator of the dot plots didn’t compare the US to the same countries in each plot.
	When looking at the dot plots, the first thing that comes to my mind is the fact that we have a lower minimum wage and higher cell service rates compared to some of the other countries shown. Within our community, and around the US as a whole, I think this could raise some controversy on why we don’t have a higher minimum wage, and lower cell service rates. I know that I certainly would want to have those two things done personally. These dot plots suggest that the US is lower in some large areas compared to other big countries around the world, so I would title this graph, “Is The United States Falling Behind in Population Well-Being?”.

comments.raw_comment:
1. I noticed in these four graphs that the United States sat in the middle for annual hours worked and annual minimum wage, but also was on the high end of cell phone cost and health expenditures. The U.S. also acts as an outlier on the graph depicting health expenditures, for it lay on the high far right of the graph. This stood out to me because most countries were in the 9 to 11 area, while the US sat at the 18 to 19 mark. 
2. As the U.S. acts as the outlier in the health expenditures graph, it makes me wonder why we reach the highest in that category with no questions asked. Is it because other countries have completely different healthcare systems in their country, or maybe it has to do more with the economy.
3. All of these graphs affect nearly every local community, including mine. That is because healthcare and minimum wage will always be the main concern in our modern society. As the prices of everyday products increase, the minimum wage stays the same. That can result in widespread debt across the country. These grapes show that the United States seems to make life harder for its citizens to succeed and be supplied with their basic needs with ease.
4. A catchy headline I would use to describe these graphs as a whole would be: “The differences borders make”

comments.raw_comment: In this week's graph, I noticed that it is depicting how the U.S.' spending and money stack up to other countries. In the graphs shown, the U.S.' cost for cellphone service and healthcare is the highest out of other countries. I can't say I'm surprised by this. I know many families struggle with healthcare prices and it honestly is disappointing to know how much less people pay for healthcare in other countries. I also notice that in the other two graphs, we seem to be in the middle of other countries for minimum wage & annual hours worked. This is interesting in relation to the prices for healthcare and cellphone services, as many other countries have higher minimum wage and lower healthcare. For other countries, I wonder what is causing them to have such low healthcare + cell phone service prices. It may come with consequences, but it truly is fascinating to see how many other countries have lower prices. We seem to have extremely expensive healthcare and cellphone prices and they're constantly going up. I also wonder how this relates to inflation rates. If our dollar's worth is inflating, how do the prices inflate to accommodate this? This impacts me and my community, as some people do struggle with healthcare, especially in this time of Covid-19. I know many families in my parent's work have lost their healthcare benefits and most of their coverage, so I really hope this can be fixed post-virus. A catchy title for this all: "America: How Our Money Stacks Up"

comments.raw_comment:
1. I notice that the United States' cell phone service costs and health expenditures exceed those of other countries by a pretty astonishing amount. What makes this more significant is that the annual hours worked and minimum wage for the US is in the middle in comparison to other countries. 
2. I wonder as to why the United States has one of the worlds highest costs for basic needs while struggling to give minimum wage to its employees. I want to know if that is because the United States tends to overprice their bills for the benefit its companies. This worries me because I want to know if companies are considering the money that the average American makes versus what they charge. 
3. This impacts my community negatively because the United States charges a lot of money for health insurance, car insurance, house insurance -- literally anything that ends with insurance -- while the average person in my community does not make that much money. I think companies need to reassess how much they are charging for lower income communities and see if they can be adjusted for them. 
4. In these graphs we can see where the United States stands in comparison to other countries on four different topics. Catchy headline: "US Finances: Overpriced or Underpaid?"

comments.raw_comment: These four graphs compare the U.S. to other countries on income and well-being. I noticed that the first (cell phone service cost-2019) and third (health expenditures-2017)  dot plots show the U.S. above any other country. With the cell phone service cost, U.S. is just above another country, whereas with the health expenditures our nation is clearly an outlier since being far above. The other two graphs, annual hours worked in 2018 and the annual minimum wage in 2018 show the U.S. in relatively the middle of the other countries. It is no surprise that we are in the middle for annual hours worked since our country doesn’t overwork the people with many receiving sabbaticals and breaks. Also, I’m not shocked that the U.S. has the highest cell phone service cost. Our country is extremely attached to their devices and is utilized for many things daily. The healthcare here is high quality and for that, drugs/medicine are costly and for the certification doctors require, they have a higher salary than other jobs. Due to these reasons, the U.S. spends a great deal on healthcare to ensure the well-being of the people. I wonder how the health expenditures have raised in all countries since the current pandemic. Has the annual minimum wage and hours of work lowered with the increase in unemployment? These graphs really display the value of money and how we utilize it for different things to overall support our country. A headline that applies to this is "Money in Different Countries".

The US measures for incomes and well-being are high compare to other countries. Why do the minimum wage of US lower than many countries when it is the country with the strongest economy. Is there a way the government can help further raise the minimum wage for the people?

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that the U.S. has the highest cellphone service cost and health expenditures, and Mexico has the greatest number of annual hours worked. While the nation with the second-highest cellphone service cost is just behind the U.S., there's a large margin between the U.S. and Switzerland in the health expenditures. The U.S. is closer to the middle of the graphs in terms of annual minimum wage and annual hours worked. 

I wonder if in any way, this gives an insight into the economic system of the U.S. With costs and expenses so high but having average minimum wages, how many families struggle with paying the bills? I also wonder how the graph would compare if all the stats were taken this year, especially with the pandemic having a huge impact on the economy. Another question I have is why the U.S. doesn't have a universal healthcare policy of some kind like the other questions. In terms of Mexico having the most annual hours worked, I wonder if that relates to how many companies bring their manufacturing out-of-country in order to lower production costs.

This impacts me and my community because this is something that people face daily when it comes to costs. In addition, many people have struggled with paying bills due to job loss as a result of the pandemic. It's also concerning to see that Americans need to spend so much money, yet it doesn't seem like that money is being used properly. 

A headline could be: "Are Americans Spending Too Much or Are the Prices Too High?"

The graphs appeared online in the article “The U.S. Is Lagging Behind Many Rich Countries These Charts Show Why. ” (URL in the release.)  By viewing the graphs online, you can see the name of the country for each point on the graphs.

After you’ve learned from others, then respond online.  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Keep noticing and wondering.  Stay tuned for the next release on Friday, Dec. 11 with moderation on Wednesday, Dec. 16.  The last graph of 2020 is about your choice for instant mastery!

comments.raw_comment: I notice that US costs were much higher in the spending categories while being relatively average in money-making categories. The US was approximately in the middle of both the annual hours worked and annual minimum wage distributions. Looking at spending costs, however, the US was by far the highest. It’s interesting to see because cellphones and healthcare are deemed necessary in modern society, but the graphs show that US worker’s wages have not increased proportionally. In terms of health expenditures, US costs were substantially higher than every other country likely being an outlier. I wonder why the US chooses private health care companies over universal health care? As shown, Switzerland had about 5% fewer health expenditures as a share of GDP, using universal health care. The US higher healthcare costs may promote the economy but could negatively impact low-income families. What are the benefits of prioritizing economy over way of life? Why has the US not raised the minimum wage to potentially compensate for these high necessity costs? The impact this has on my community is that in the US, there is an immense amount of pressure to live an expensive lifestyle no matter economic status. We in need of employment, work for minimum wage which companies have kept low. However, companies, in turn, raise prices on necessities such as cellphone costs along with our costly privatized healthcare system. My headline is, “The American Dream Is No Longer Looking Very Dreamy."

1.) What do I notice? I noticed how the U.S took first place out of two of the graphs, the cell phone service cost, and the health expenditures. The U.S. did roughly average when it came to minimum wage and annual hours worked placing them around where most countries are. Next thing I noticed was the different times these graphs were based upon, and how the U.S seemed to be an outlier in some graphs.
2) What do I wonder? One thing I wonder is whether or not the graphs would change if they were all from the same year or even this year, and see whether or not the pandemic affected these graphs. I also wonder why are we at the top of health expenditures? Shouldn't a well-leading country in the world be trying its absolute best to be lowering those costs and make it more accessible to all people especially since we are roughly average in our minimum wage.
3) How does this affect me? 
 This obviously affects me in the path I'm heading towards later on in life. Whenever I'm going to pay for my phone bill or health coverage, It's going to be way higher than it is in some countries. On top of that annual hours are low, so this can really make students, or immigrants from other countries starting a life in America extremely tough. 
4) Showing how the U.S. is seeming to lead almost negatively in some of these graphs, my title might be "Is America the best, at being the worst?!"

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that the distribution of health expenditures is strongly right-skewed. The US is far out on the right tail, away from the main cluster of points between 8 and 12%. It appears to be a high outlier. In the graph of cell phone service where the US is also the highest value, it is unlikely to be an outlier since the distribution has a greater spread. Overall, the US has extremely high costs while only landing around the upper middle in terms of minimum wage and hours worked compared to other countries. 
I wonder why health expenditures in the US are so absurdly high compared to other countries. Everyone knows that the US has expensive health care, one example being the insane cost of insulin. However, it seems like not much is being done to fix this issue. I also wonder how these graphs would change if data from past years was shown.
This impacts me by reminding me that as a US citizen, I have to work harder than in other countries due to the higher costs of living. As someone who has been though quite a few medical issues in my life, it’s disheartening to see how much of my income will have to go into health care. In my community, people with chronic illnesses or other severe health concerns may be even more negatively affected.
These graphs demonstrate how despite the US being a rich, first-world country, life might not be that great for the average citizen compared with other countries. A title idea could be “Is Life In The US As Great As It Seems?”

comments.raw_comment: One thing I noticed was that in relation to other countries, the dots which represented the U.S. were fairly scattered among the four graphs. However, the U.S. tended to fall into the upper half of the graph, regardless of which countries preceded and succeeded it. The U.S. has the highest cellphone service cost and highest health expenditures, but fall in the middle for annual hours worked and annual minimum wage. One thing I wonder is how our dot placement in these four graphs would differ if the same data was collected in 2020, due to how much the economy has changed due to COVID-19. Another thing I wonder is how the other countries that appear on the graph were chosen since only a few countries appear. One last thing I wonder is why the prices for phones, healthcare, and other services are so high when in relation to other countries, our annual income is not as high for how long and hard people are working. This data impacts my community as it shows how although the United States is viewed as a country of wealth and opportunities, that compared to other places, people can end up spending a lot more on services that they shouldn’t have to spend so much on. While it is true that overall, the U.S. is a wealthy country, residents tend to spend a lot more money on necessities than people in other countries. These graphs compare the U.S. to other countries in relation to expenditures and income. A catchy title could be “U.S. Expenditure and Revenue: How Do They Compare?”

What do you notice?
The U.S. falls on the right side of the distribution in the “Cellphone service cost in 2019” graph as well as the “Health expenditures in 2017, share of G.D.P.” graph. On the other two graphs, “Annual hours worked in 2018” and Annual minimum wage in 2018”, the U.S. falls on the center of the distribution.
What do you wonder?
I wonder how different these graphs would look if they were from this year. I wonder how much the pandemic has affected these categories.
 What impact does this have on you and your community?
I think a lot of people believe that the U.S. is the most consistently wealthy country; a lot of people don’t realize we also have a massive wealth gap. The result that stood out to me the most was that the U.S. falls very far to the right of the distribution in the “Health expenditures in 2017, share of G.D.P.” graph, while the other countries fall to the left of the distribution. I would guess this is because we have one of the most expensive healthcare systems. It’s truly eye-opening to see just how much more we pay for healthcare.

I wonder if the graph depicting the annual hours world was calculated with only the amount of hours adult workers work or if it includes teenage/student workers. I also wonder why the average hours worked a day can be calculated for about 6.92 hours a day on a five day work week if business hours typically are 9 hours a day.

As a high schooler having to work less hours than the average annual hours, I would make very little money working on minimum wage in comparison to what I need to pay for college.

1. I notice that in these graphs, the United States is either towards the middle of the data or on the far right. The categories, “Cellphone service costs in 2019” and “Health Expenditures in 2017, share of G.D.P” show this. These two clearly show the United States to be the priciest country out of those surveyed. For the other categories, “Annual hours worked in 2017” and “Annual minimum wage in 2018” the United States is in the center of the distribution. 
2. I wonder how other countries rank across all of the categories. Though the graphs show reference countries for each category, it’s hard to gauge truly how the United States compares when each country only appears in one category. I wonder if the United States would look better or worse in comparison to other countries if say China, Italy, and Brazil were shown for reference in each category instead of just one.
3. I think this graph has an impact on a larger more continental scale. For everyone in America, it gives them a better understanding of how the country really compares to those around them and might help people (most likely younger) get a better sense on where they might want to live. For example, if someone is very keen on free healthcare, they might realize that the United States is probably not the best country for them to live in.
4. These graphs compare the United States to varieties of countries around the world in a series of categories. Catchy headline: “The Highs and the Lows”

It would be interesting to know why other countries had higher annual minimum wages and more annual hours worked. I would like to know if there are any common or uncommon jobs worked within each country.
My community and I were paying the most for cell phone service in 2019. Our country was charging everyone much more than any other country was charging their citizens. Jobs in the United States during 2018 paid their workers the average annual minimum wage amount. Workers in some countries received more money but workers in other countries received less.

2. I wonder what society is like in other countries displayed based on their position in the graphs.  For example, in Switzerland or France, do they have more extra money to spend since their cell phone and health expenditures are low?

This affects my family like it affects many others - and will significantly affect my generation when we are eventually in college and beyond.  In the US, those making minimum wage find it extremely difficult to pay for necessities and have money left over, which is clearly shown by the graphs.

1. I notice that the United States ranks high in spending habits but average in compensation and working habits. According to the first graph, the United States had the maximum cell phone service cost in 2019. Also, the United States seems to be an upper bound outlier in the health expenditures in 2017 category. However, the United States falls in roughly the middle of the spectrum, closer to the median, when it comes to annual hours worked in 2018 and annual minimum wage in 2018. 
2. I wonder why the United States has such a high ingrained sense of consumerism since worker compensation does not seem to promote this? Why does the United States continue to rely on mainly-privatized health expenditures if it clearly puts its people at disadvantages? Finally, I wonder why different countries are labeled in each graph? Did the statistician purposefully integrate bias?
3. These graphs show that members of my community may feel pressure to sustain an expensive lifestyle from lower incomes. The graphs show that “essentials,” such as health care and cell phones, are not proportionally charged to what many workers make in a year. These patterns negatively affect me. I feel pressure to participate in high spending habits, even though I am paid below the United States' average value for minimum wage.
4. “High United States Spending Patterns Despite Average Worker Compensation”

A) I noticed that the US is placed near or slightly above the centers of the distributions for hours worked and minimum wage. When it came to basic services, I noticed that the US was the maximum value in both distributions (costs of cell service and healthcare). I was most interested in Health Expenditures as a share of GDP. I noticed that the US pays WAY more in healthcare costs than other countries. I hear a lot of people criticizing ideas like Medicare-for-All by saying that it’s ‘too expensive.’ If that’s the case, why is it that other countries, many of which have universal healthcare, have less costly healthcare systems than the US (as a % of GDP)?
B) I wonder why some of the points in each plot are labeled and some aren’t. For example, why are Canada and Switzerland labeled in the healthcare plot? Some of the labeled points seem to be maximums or minimums of the distributions, but the ones in the middle confuse me. Some plots have three points labeled in the middle, others two.
C) Americans have to pay way more for basic services than people in other countries. I think part of that is that many other countries have better social safety nets and public services than the US. Lack of these basic services can be detrimental to many working class Americans.
D) “Ironically, the Land of the Free Is Pretty Expensive.”
In general, while American workers are paid about what one would expect and work a reasonable amount of hours, they have a much higher cost of living.

comments.raw_comment:
We noticed:
-America's minimum wage is considerably lower than that of the other developed countries on the graph such as Ireland and Australia
-America has much higher expenditures/costs than other nations

We wondered:
-What impact does this have? For example, Germany works less than the US; are their health and stress levels better and lower, respectively?
-Does cell phone service affect people's ability to communicate?
-Would the US need to spend less on healthcare if costs weren't so high?
-How does healthcare cost correlate to quality of care in other countries?
-Why do we pay our workers less for more hours, and charge them more for services?

The impact this has on our community is:
-High health expenditures likely correlates with better health outcomes as long as money is being used efficiently
-High health expenditures mean more people have medicare/medicaid
-Lower minimum wage likely corresponds to more struggles for citizens. If a community has a lower minimum wage, more of its citizens are likely to be impoverished.

Our title is "Green Makes the World Go Around".
